articleHeadline: Weasel Bite Linked to Deadly Tick-Borne Virus in Rare Chinese Case
articleSummary: Five days after a bite from a Siberian weasel (Mustela sibirica) in Dalian, Liaoning Province, China, a 55-year-old woman developed fever, malaise and diarrhea. Laboratory tests showed thrombocytopenia and multi-organ dysfunction. On day 12 of illness, metagenomic next-generation sequencing detected SFTSV (severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus) in peripheral blood, confirming infection. SFTSV, a Bandavirus in Phenuiviridae, is traditionally tick-borne and primarily transmitted by Haemaphysalis longicornis; outbreaks have been reported in China, South Korea, Japan and Vietnam, with case-fatality rates ranging about 5-20%. While ticks are the main vector, the virus circulates in cattle, goats, dogs, cats, and wild mammals. This case documents a direct mammal-to-human transmission via a bite, implying that wild carnivores could contribute to human exposure, particularly in rural northeastern China.

Past outbreaks in eastern DRC and Uganda show high pediatric CFRs, commonly around 70–78% for under-fives. WHO urges child-friendly treatment-centre designs and keeping families with patients.

articleSummary: Filter-mating combined with nanopore selective sequencing (FM-NSS) enriches conjugative antibiotic-resistance plasmids from total DNA in wastewater, avoiding plasmid DNA extraction. Leptospirosis is caused by bacteria in the urine of infected animals, mainly rats, with elevated risk during floods when water and mud can be contaminated. Infection occurs via contact with contaminated material of wounds or mucous membranes; prolonged skin exposure also poses risk. Common symptoms include fever, headache, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, and muscle pain; severe cases may cause jaundice, kidney failure, hemorrhages, and respiratory distress. articleSummary: Two Changhua County, Taiwan residents who joined a group tour to Phu Quoc Island, Vietnam (Sept 12–15) were confirmed with dengue fever upon return, classed as imported cases. Prevention includes screened or air-conditioned accommodations, long-sleeved light clothing outdoors, and government-approved repellents. Post-return vector control should follow “inspect, drain, clean, and scrub” to remove standing water and mosquito eggs, reducing community transmission risk.

articleHeadline: New Antibody Tests Outperform PCR in Detecting Devastating Rice Panicle
articleSummary: Dot-ELISA and CGICS, developed by Zhejiang University researchers, detect Burkholderia glumae and B. plantarii, the primary agents of rice bacterial panicle blight (RBPB). The serological tests outperform conventional PCR in sensitivity and require no expensive lab equipment, enabling field and port screening. Antibody pairs: 4A7/8C5 target B. glumae; 12B5/14B3 target B. plantarii; both show high specificity with no cross-reaction to non-target Burkholderia or other rice pathogens. Detection limits: 1.96×10^4 CFU/mL for either pathogen, roughly 2–4× more sensitive than PCR (3.91×10^4 and 7.81×10^4 CFU/mL). In infected grain homogenates, positives at 1:7680 dilution, twice PCR sensitivity (1:3840). RBPB, described in Japan in the 1950s, is now widespread in Africa, Asia, North and South America; Vietnam 1992 outbreak yielded up to 75% yield losses, while typical losses are around 15%.
notes: 疾患名『Melioidosis』は誤り。記事はイネの細菌性穂枯病（rice bacterial panicle blight）に関する農業・植物病理学の研究であり、ヒトの感染症サーベイランスの対象ではない。影響カテゴリも『plants』であることから、感染症危機管理の観点では対象外と判断。
